notes: Building on the Joule–Thomson effect, the cooling capacity of the released air also depends on where the energy goes.
If we can further reduce its enthalpy during release, we can achieve a lower temperature and greater cooling capacity.
There are two main approaches to maximizing cooling capacity.
One is to use an expander to convert some of the energy into shaft work, producing colder air.
The other is to use a vortex tube to separate the air into hot and cold streams, making the air at the cold outlet even colder.
We used a scuba tank as the air source and tested two pathways:
direct release after a single pressure-reduction stage, and release through a vortex tube after two pressure-reduction stages.
We then used a Kestrel to measure temperature changes downstream.

text: Outlet cooling in two recorded trials
notes: We first measured the temperature change right at the nozzle outlet.
For direct release, the temperature dropped from 26 to 22.2 degrees Celsius—a reduction of 3.8 degrees.
The vortex tube produced a larger temperature drop, from 22 to 5.3 degrees Celsius—a reduction of 16.7 degrees.
Based on this comparison, we continued with the vortex tube and
tested how different nozzles affect cold-air delivery at 0.2 and 0.5 meters downstream.
We tested three types: an adjustable nozzle that produces a focused jet, a high-flow nozzle, and a fan-shaped spray nozzle.
The indoor comparison showed that at 0.2 meters downstream, the high-flow and fan-shaped nozzles produced greater temperature reductions than the adjustable nozzle.
The high-flow nozzle performed best, reaching a minimum temperature of 19.6 degrees Celsius.
At 0.5 meters, the measured temperatures were similar across all three nozzles.
We tested airflow at three locations: the face, the top of the head, and the back of the neck.
The setup uses a 20-centimeter nozzle-to-target distance and a 30-second release.

notes: Option 1 retains the current scuba cylinder and first-stage regulator. The air hose does not set pressure; a dedicated compatible downstream pressure-control component would be needed to supply the vortex tube at the manufacturer's required pressure. The conceptual chain is cylinder, first-stage regulator, verified pressure control to approximately 6.5–6.9 bar(g), dry-air/flow verification, vortex tube, and controlled cold outlet. The project measured 25°C to 16°C at the short-path nozzle outlet, not immediately at the first-stage outlet. The approximately -15°C value is an arithmetic scenario: 16°C minus the approximately 31°C momentary cold-end split shown in the YouTube demonstration. Vortex-tube performance is not necessarily linear with inlet temperature, so this value must be tested and must not be treated as expected delivered performance.

Option 2 uses the Kaneez 10 HP 4-in-1 package as a direct low-pressure dry-air source. Vendor-listed values are 8–10 bar and 1.0–1.2 m³/min with receiver, refrigerated dryer and filters, but the exact model, ISO 1217 FAD at 6.9 bar, pressure dew point and continuous-duty operation remain to be confirmed in writing. The approximately 25°C to -6°C benchmark comes from the YouTube demonstration, not from the Kaneez package.

Both paths require flow and pressure measurement, moisture control, noise and hot-exhaust management, cold-end temperature history, icing/condensation assessment and qualified engineering review before public demonstration. These are conceptual test architectures, not approved operating instructions.

Project measurements supplied by the user on 2026-09-25. Ambient/start temperature: 25°C. Full path: 21°C at nozzle and 24°C at 0.5 m. Short path: 16°C at nozzle and 23°C at 0.5 m. Valve operation was manual and mass flow was not measured.

Thermodynamic framing: a regulator is approximated as an adiabatic throttling device with near-constant stagnation enthalpy; the nozzle converts part of stagnation enthalpy into kinetic energy. This slide does not claim a measured Joule–Thomson coefficient or cooling capacity.

Mechanism boundary: a vortex tube has no shaft work. It separates the inlet into a low-enthalpy cold stream and a higher-enthalpy hot reject stream; energy is redistributed between the two streams. A turboexpander approaches isentropic expansion and extracts shaft work, lowering total enthalpy and total temperature of the gas passing through the turbine. Neither mechanism alone establishes pedestrian cooling performance.
